feat: optional wake-on-PS-button HID for Windows S3 sleep

Adds an opt-in build flavor (-DENABLE_WAKE_HID=ON) that lets the dongle
wake a sleeping Windows host from S3 when the controller's PS button is
pressed. When the build flag is on:

- TinyUSB exposes a second HID interface (boot keyboard, EP 0x85)
  alongside the existing gamepad interface. CFG_TUD_HID becomes 2.
- The configuration descriptor advertises remote-wakeup capability
  (bmAttributes 0xC0 -> 0xE0); wTotalLength and bNumInterfaces are
  bumped accordingly.
- A small FSM in src/wake.cpp tracks host suspend/resume via TinyUSB
  callbacks, watches the BT 0x31 input report for a PS-button rising
  edge while suspended, calls tud_remote_wakeup(), then injects a
  single F15 keypress + release. F15 has no default Windows binding,
  so a stray fire never inserts characters or triggers shortcuts.
- The FSM is non-blocking (time_us_64 deltas only) and watchdog-safe;
  a 5 s timeout in REQUESTED guards against tud_remote_wakeup never
  resuming when the user has not enabled the wake checkbox in Device
  Manager.

Scope is S3 only; Modern Standby (S0ix) is intentionally out of scope.
Default builds are byte-identical to before (entire feature is behind
ENABLE_WAKE_HID).

fix: PS button is at hid_input[9] bit 0, not [8] bit 0

The original wake_on_bt_input watched hid_input[8] & 0x01 as the PS-button
edge, but byte 8 bit 0 of the DualSense BT 0x31 input report (after
main.cpp's `data + 3` skip) is L1, not PS. PS lives at byte 9 bit 0.

Verified with a diagnostic firmware that, while the host was suspended,
dumped the first 12 bytes of every BT report whose button bytes changed.
Pressing each individual button on the controller and observing which
byte/bit changed gave a complete map:

    byte 7 low nibble: D-pad direction (0x08 idle)
    byte 7 high nibble: square / cross / circle / triangle (0x10..0x80)
    byte 8: L1, R1, L2 click, R2 click, share, options, L3, R3
    byte 9: PS (bit 0), touchpad click (bit 1), mute (bit 2)

The previous code "worked" because mashing buttons usually toggled L1
(or because L1 itself was sometimes pressed in the same gesture as PS),
which fired our byte-8-bit-0 edge and triggered remote wakeup. Pressing
PS strictly alone would not wake the host. Reading the correct bit
makes the documented PS-only trigger actually behave as documented.

feat: wake on any controller button + speculative remote-wakeup

Two changes in wake_on_bt_input that together make wake-on-PS reliable
in real-world use:

1. Trigger on any change in the DualSense button bytes (7, 8, and 9),
   not strictly on the PS bit. The Sony controller's BT radio enters a
   low-power sniff mode when idle; the PS button alone often does not
   wake the radio out of sniff while shoulder/face buttons reliably do.
   So in practice the first BT report after S3 is whichever button the
   user happened to press to wake the radio -- and PS itself counts as
   "any button" so the documented single-press UX still works. Without
   this, users had to mash multiple buttons before one happened to land
   on the bit our edge detector watched.

2. Call tud_remote_wakeup() speculatively even from WAKE_IDLE and
   WAKE_DONE state, not only after tud_suspend_cb has fired. TinyUSB
   returns true only when the host has the bus in USB suspend; otherwise
   it is a clean no-op. This protects against the case where
   tud_suspend_cb did not fire on the device (e.g. a powered hub between
   the host and the dongle masking the suspend signal from downstream).
   On success the FSM transitions into WAKE_REQUESTED and proceeds with
   the keystroke as normal. Without this, hub-masked-suspend setups
   could not wake the host even though all the underlying USB signaling
   would have worked.

prev_ps_bit is replaced with prev_b7 / prev_b8 / prev_b9 (initial
values 0x08 / 0x00 / 0x00 = controller fully released). tud_suspend_cb
and wake_on_bt_disconnect reset all three. The minimum report length
check goes from len < 9 to len < 10 since we now read byte 9.

fix: call wake_on_bt_input on all polling modes, not only mode 2

Upstream commit `cmd: poll rate switch` (0d32db4) rewrote on_bt_data so
that polling_rate_mode != 2 takes an early-return path that skips the
critical_section_enter / report_dirty branch. After the wake-on-PS
feature was rebased on top of that, our wake_on_bt_input() call sat on
the late path -- meaning the wake FSM only observed BT reports when
the user happened to be in polling mode 2. On the default polling mode,
wake_on_bt_input was never called, so during host suspend no button
edge fired and the wake never happened.

Symptom on UART:
  [wake] tud_suspend_cb remote_wakeup_en=1 prev_state=IDLE
  [wake] -> PENDING_PRESS
  ... silence forever; no [wake] button event line ...

Fix: hoist the wake_on_bt_input() call above the polling-mode branch.
The wake feature must observe every report regardless of polling mode.
The function is a no-op when not host-suspended and is cheap to call,
so this has no perf impact in the common case.

feat: MS OS 2.0 SelectiveSuspendEnabled to unblock wake-from-S3

The dongle is a composite USB device with an Audio Class function. By
default Windows audio engine policy keeps USB audio devices at D0 even
during system S3, which prevents the host from selectively suspending
the whole composite. Without selective suspend the bus never goes to
USB suspend, tud_suspend_cb never fires, and tud_remote_wakeup() refuses
to signal -- breaking wake-on-PS on machines with this policy. Confirmed
on Windows 11 with a bottom-up bisection (full dongle minus audio class
suspends correctly; full dongle as-shipped does not).

This commit adds Microsoft OS 2.0 descriptors carried through a BOS
descriptor, instructing Windows to set SelectiveSuspendEnabled=1 on
the audio function (interface 0). Verified at install-time:

  HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB\VID_054C&PID_0CE6&MI_00\
       <instance>\Device Parameters\SelectiveSuspendEnabled = dword:1

After enumeration Windows now selectively suspends the composite,
tud_suspend_cb fires on S3 entry, and pressing the controller's PS
button wakes the host as designed.

Changes:
- src/usb_descriptors.c: bcdUSB 0x0200 -> 0x0210 under ENABLE_WAKE_HID
  (USB 2.1 is the prerequisite for the host to request BOS); BOS
  descriptor with one MS OS 2.0 platform capability; 88-byte MS OS 2.0
  descriptor set (set header + configuration subset + audio function
  subset + registry property feature); tud_descriptor_bos_cb and
  tud_vendor_control_xfer_cb that returns the descriptor set when the
  host asks (vendor request bRequest=0x01, wIndex=7).
- src/tusb_config.h: CFG_TUD_VENDOR=1 under ENABLE_WAKE_HID so TinyUSB
  routes vendor control transfers to the new callback. No vendor-class
  interface is added to the configuration descriptor.

The change is entirely behind ENABLE_WAKE_HID. Default builds are
byte-for-byte identical to the previous wake-on-ps tip.

Note for users: Windows caches device-install state, so on machines
that previously enumerated the dongle without this descriptor, the
registry property is not retroactively applied. Uninstall the dongle
from Device Manager (and tick "delete the driver software" if offered)
before flashing this firmware to force a fresh install.

test: add WAKE_DEBUG flag for wake-FSM tracing over UART

Adds an opt-in -DWAKE_DEBUG=ON build flag (default OFF) that prints
wake-FSM transitions to the existing UART stdout at the key points:

- tud_suspend_cb / tud_resume_cb fire (with prev state).
- PS button rising edge detected and tud_remote_wakeup() return value.
- Each FSM state transition (REQUESTED -> KEY_DOWN -> KEY_UP_SENT
  -> DONE) and the corresponding tud_hid_n_report() outcome.
- Hard-rate-limited 1Hz heartbeat lines while waiting for hid_n_ready
  during the post-resume window so a stuck FSM is observable but
  the UART can't be flooded enough to starve the watchdog.
- 5-second WAKE_REQUESTED timeout when the host never resumes.

Default-off with no impact on shipped firmware. Useful for verifying
the wake feature end-to-end on systems where MS OS 2.0 should have
made selective-suspend work, and for diagnosing failures.

fix(wake): keep USB alive across BT off, retry F15 against wake-and-resleep

Two related fixes to wake-from-S3 on machines where the user power-cycles
the DualSense while the PC is asleep.

1. bt.cpp: when ENABLE_WAKE_HID is on, do not call tud_disconnect() on
   BT disconnect. Upstream hides the dongle from USB whenever no
   controller is paired, but that breaks wake: with no USB device on
   the bus while the PC is in S3, there is nothing to signal remote
   wakeup when the user turns the controller back on. Staying on the
   bus lets tud_suspend_cb fire and tud_remote_wakeup() reach the host
   later. Behavior with ENABLE_WAKE_HID off is unchanged.

2. wake.cpp: the F15 keypress now uses longer settle and key-hold times
   and is sent twice with a 200 ms gap. Without this, on some Windows
   configurations the host briefly resumes from S3 to deliver the wake
   notification, finds no input it considers user activity (the
   keypress lands during USB re-init and is dropped), then immediately
   re-suspends. The longer hold gives Windows a full HID polling cycle
   to consume the keystroke, and the retry covers the brief-resume
   case. The retry path sends the second keydown directly instead of
   re-entering WAKE_REQUESTED, so it does not stall waiting for a
   resume signal that already fired.

Misleading WAKE_REQUESTED timeout message updated to reflect that the
host may already have woken when the timeout fires.

Add Windows build script and reusable CI build

Many users can view the project but cannot build the Pico2W firmware.
This adds two things to lower that barrier:

- tools/build-windows.ps1: a one-command Windows 11 builder (no WSL).

  TinyUSB, and builds ds5-bridge.uf2. Run from a checkout or fully
  standalone (it clones the repo itself). Idempotent; -Variant
  debug|wake; -Repo/-Ref to build a fork or specific ref. Validated
  end-to-end on a clean Windows 11 Windows Sandbox.

  build factored out of release.yml's duplicated steps (standard +
  debug UF2, optional release upload, -DVERSION passthrough).
  release.yml now calls it - no behavior change.

fix(batt-led): force LED off + disarm on disconnect

The low-battery blink would stay frozen mid-cycle (or briefly resume
during reconnect retries) after a controller died and lost connection,
because the stale-report check stopped toggling but never turned the
LED off, and the cached interrupt_in_data[52] still read low.

New `battery_led_on_disconnect()` clears blink state, forces the LED
off, and zeros last_report_us so the stale-check early-return blocks
any new blink until a fresh 0x31 report arrives on the next connection.
Called from bt.cpp's HCI_EVENT_DISCONNECTION_COMPLETE handler.

Stale-check in the tick also now forces LED off when it fires while a
blink was in progress (defense in depth for unclean disconnects).

Same bug exists in upstream awalol/DS5Dongle (their battery_led.cpp is
byte-identical to ours pre-fix) — Sura Academy reported it in their
Discord. Plan to send this back as a PR after we validate it locally.

build: add Waveshare RP2350B-Plus-W as a build target

The Waveshare RP2350B-Plus-W is a Pico 2 W form-factor board with a
USB-C port, 16MB flash, RP2350B (48-pin, 41 GPIOs), and the same
Raspberry Pi RM2 wireless module as the Pico 2 W. Several users in
issue #12 have asked about USB-C-equipped Pico 2 W alternatives;
this is one answer.

The board needs a custom CMake target because Waveshare wired the
CYW43/RM2 module to a different set of RP2350 GPIOs from the official
Pico 2 W: WL_REG_ON on GP36 (vs GP23), WL_DATA* on GP37, WL_CS on GP38,
WL_CLOCK on GP39. A stock pico2_w build can't drive the radio on this
board because it asserts REG_ON on the wrong pin.

Changes:
  - boards/headers/waveshare_rp2350b_plus_w.h: board header for the
    Waveshare RP2350B-Plus-W. Sourced from Waveshare's official demo zip
    on their wiki (BSD-3-Clause, RPi Trading Ltd copyright), shipped
    here because upstream pico-sdk does not yet include it. Adds a
    pico_board_cmake_set(PICO_CYW43_SUPPORTED, 1) directive that was
    absent in the upstream Waveshare-supplied file -- needed for
    pico-sdk to build pico_cyw43_arch and expose its headers.
  - CMakeLists.txt: new WAVESHARE_RP2350B_PLUS_W_BUILD option (mutually
    exclusive with PICO_W_BUILD); when set, PICO_BOARD becomes
    waveshare_rp2350b_plus_w and PICO_BOARD_HEADER_DIRS is extended to
    include boards/headers/. Same clock/audio config as the Pico 2 W
    path. Four diagnostic message(STATUS ...) lines print the resolved
    board configuration during cmake configure so the selected target
    is verifiable from build output.
  - boards/build_waveshare_rp2350b_plus_w.sh: convenience build script.

Verified: builds cleanly against pinned SDK 2.2.0 + TinyUSB 0.20.0 for
both the default Pico 2 W target and the new Waveshare target. The
diagnostic STATUS lines and CMakeCache.txt both confirm PICO_BOARD
resolves to waveshare_rp2350b_plus_w in the new target. The resulting
ds5-bridge.elf contains 'waveshare_rp2350b_plus_w' as a string and not
'pico2_w', confirming the binary was built with the correct board
definition.

Not verified: actual board behavior. Hardware not yet on hand.

build: declare boot2_w25q080 as default boot stage 2 for Waveshare

The Waveshare-supplied header has the C-side declaration
(#define PICO_BOOT_STAGE2_CHOOSE_W25Q080 1) but is missing the
CMake-side declaration that tells pico-sdk's build system to link
the W25Q080-specific boot stage 2 instead of falling back to the
generic boot2. Compare against the SDK's own pico2_w.h, which has
both:

    pico_board_cmake_set(PICO_DEFAULT_BOOT_STAGE2, boot2_w25q080)

Without this line, waveshare-test-2 boots successfully past CYW43
init (LED on the wireless module can be driven, confirming wireless
came up), then crashes during runtime in a watchdog reboot loop
that produces the 3-blink pattern from main.cpp when
watchdog_caused_reboot() returns true. The crash symptom is
consistent with generic boot2 reading flash correctly during initial
XIP cache fill but failing at higher speeds or specific commands
required during runtime.

Verified at the build-system level (CMakeCache.txt now shows
PICO_DEFAULT_BOOT_STAGE2:STRING=boot2_w25q080) but not yet verified
on real hardware on our end — still no Waveshare board in hand.

fix(waveshare): correct schematic mismatches in board header

The Waveshare-supplied board header contained three values inconsistent
with the actual board schematic:

- PICO_VSYS_PIN was 43; the schematic shows VSYS_SENSE on GPIO46
  (ADC6). Confirmed by the Waveshare schematic PDF and the
  arduino-pico variant for this board.

- CYW43_WL_GPIO_VBUS_PIN was defined as 2 (CYW43 chip GPIO2). On the
  Pico 2 W this pin senses VBUS through the wireless chip, but on
  this board VBUS detection is on the RP2350 side (via Q2 WNM2021-3
  and a resistor divider; schematic net VBUS_DET), not through the
  RM2/CYW43 module. The macro is removed.

- CYW43_USES_VSYS_PIN was set, telling the SDK that CYW43 and VSYS
  sensing share a GPIO and require cooperative access. On Pico 2 W
  this is correct (VSYS sense and WL_CLOCK both on GPIO29). On this
  board VSYS sense is on GPIO46 and WL_CLOCK is on GPIO39, so no
  sharing occurs. The macro is removed.

These changes do not address the audio static issue observed on
Waveshare hardware (verified empirically), but they are real
correctness fixes relative to the schematic and prevent the SDK
from making wrong assumptions about pin sharing and VBUS sensing.

fix(waveshare): force boot2 execution to fix flash XIP for Puya flash

On RP2350, boot stage 2 assembly is compiled into the binary but is
NOT executed by default — the bootrom auto-configures XIP based on
probing the flash chip via SFDP. This means PICO_FLASH_SPI_CLKDIV=4
(cherry-picked from upstream/dev for the 320MHz overclock) was being
silently ignored.

The Waveshare RP2350B-Plus-W ships with a Puya PY25Q128HA flash chip
despite the schematic listing a Winbond W25Q128JVSIQ. The RP2350
bootrom auto-detected this Puya chip and configured QMI with CLKDIV=3
and Fast Read Dual I/O (0xBB):

  [QMI] timing=0x60007203 rfmt=0x00009154 rcmd=0x000000bb

At the project's 320MHz overclocked sys_clk, CLKDIV=3 puts flash SPI
at 106.7MHz, over Puya's 104MHz spec for the 0xBB Fast Read Dual I/O
command at default 4 dummy cycles. This caused intermittent XIP read
corruption that manifested as severely choppy audio (the audio path
requires sustained high-bandwidth flash access while lower-bandwidth
operations like Bluetooth pairing and HID input tolerated the
occasional bad byte).

Setting PICO_EMBED_XIP_SETUP=1 forces the SDK to embed and execute
boot2_w25q080, which programs CLKDIV=4 (80MHz flash SPI, well within
Puya spec) and switches to Fast Read Quad I/O (0xEB), matching the
Pico 2 W's flash configuration exactly. Audio quality after this
change is verified to sound identical to Pico 2 W.

Scoped to Waveshare build only; Pico 2 W's bootrom auto-config
already works correctly for its Winbond W25Q32 flash and should not
be disturbed.

References:
- pico-sdk issue #1903 (RP2350 boot2 never run by default)
- forum thread on PICO_EMBED_XIP_SETUP requirement
- Puya PY25Q128HA datasheet V2.2 (max 104MHz for 0xBB at default DC)

fix(bt): restart inquiry and LED blink on disconnect

After bb61e00 ("fix: led blink after connected") the disconnect handler
in src/bt.cpp no longer calls gap_inquiry_start(30), and the new
bt_inquiring flag is never set back to true. This produces two
regressions visible on disconnect (controller powered off or out of
range):

1. Functional: After the controller disconnects, the dongle stops
   actively scanning for new controllers. gap_connectable_control(1)
   and gap_discoverable_control(1) remain enabled, so previously-paired
   controllers can still initiate reconnection in some cases, but the
   inquiry-based discovery path is broken. A freshly-unpaired controller
   or a different DualSense cannot be discovered.

2. Visual: The bt_inquiring_led() blink function returns early when
   bt_inquiring is false, so the LED stays solid-off after disconnect
   regardless of whether the dongle should be actively looking for a
   controller.

Re-add gap_inquiry_start(30) and set bt_inquiring = true in
HCI_EVENT_DISCONNECTION_COMPLETE to restore both behaviors.

  re-pair, fresh controller cannot pair

  re-pairs cleanly on PS button, fresh controller discoverable

perf(audio): RAM-resident mem ops + gate core1 log (Phase B.5)

Remove the last flash code core1 executes during steady-state audio, so a
gateless BOOTSEL poll (which briefly floats QSPI CSn) cannot corrupt an
in-flight flash fetch on core 1.

core1's audio loop calls memcpy/memset every frame, directly and inside
libopus. On RP2350 the Pico SDK uses newlib's flash memcpy/memset; the
pico/ROM mem-ops variant does not link (RP2350's bootrom no longer exports
ROM_FUNC_MEMCPY/MEMSET). So src/ram_mem.c provides strong memcpy/memset/
memmove overrides placed in .time_critical (RAM) via __not_in_flash_func,
built with -fno-builtin -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns so the copy
loops are not lowered back into self-recursive memcpy/memset calls.

Also gate mic_proc's opus-decode-failure printf behind ENABLE_VERBOSE: the
newlib formatting chain lives in flash, so an unconditional log would put a
flash path back on core 1. Release builds compile it out.

After this, core1's executed steady-state path is 100% RAM: the only flash
functions still reachable from speaker_proc/mic_proc are FORTIFY-check,
assert, panic, and one-time init handlers that do not run during normal
audio. Provable coverage of those is the multicore_lockout job, deferred to
the BOOTSEL feature PR.

Verified at 150 MHz / no OC: memcpy/memset/memmove at 0x20xxxxxx; ~95 KiB
heap headroom; audio (mic + speaker + 3.5mm) confirmed good on hardware.

duplicated into both channels, so the format matches the real DS5 in every case

They now ship in the base firmware, gated at runtime: new enable_wake config field (offset 20, config v3->v4); the HID keyboard interface (last descriptor block) is presented only when wake OR Game Bar is on; REMOTE_WAKEUP + MS OS 2.0 BOS only when wake is on. Both off -> enumeration byte-identical to the old base. Game Bar is decoupled from wake (no REMOTE_WAKEUP), avoiding the Linux/Wine libusb-grab issue for non-wake users.

feat(bt): BOOTSEL pair/clear with audio-aware gate

- Quick click: restart inquiry (recover from 38s pairing timeout
  without unplugging the dongle)
- Hold ~1.5s: clear stored link keys, persist BD addr blacklist,
  and LED triple-flash to confirm
- Persistent blacklist via BTstack TLV (tag 0x424C434B 'BLCK')
- Blacklist enforced in HCI_CONNECTION_COMPLETE handler

Why the gate: bt_bootsel_check() polls BOOTSEL by briefly floating
QSPI CSn (~10us). With no controller connected there is no audio
path, so polling is harmless. Once a controller pairs (hid_interrupt_cid
set), the gate suppresses polling because floating CSn corrupts XIP
fetches on core 1 where the Opus encoder is running, producing audible
buzz and link instability.

Investigation: tested proper multicore lockout coordination
(flash_safe_execute_core_init + core 1 registered as victim). The SDK
mechanism works as documented (core 1 is paused in a RAM-resident
tight loop during the CSn float), but the pauses themselves disrupt
the audio path enough to cause issues. The gate is the simpler,
more reliable solution and matches the pattern used in
wasdwasd0105/PicoW-usb2bt-audio.

feat(flash): park core1 during BOOTSEL flash access (real multicore lockout)

On master PICO_FLASH_ASSUME_CORE1_SAFE=1 makes flash_safe_execute() skip the
multicore lockout, so it is a no-op for core1 safety. Set it to 0 and register
core1 as a flash-safe victim (flash_safe_execute_core_init() in core1_entry) so
the BOOTSEL CSn float actually freezes core1 for its duration -- it can no longer
fetch from XIP flash mid-access. This is the safety mechanism that lets the
BOOTSEL button be polled while audio is streaming on core1.

fix(usb): ride out hub-induced suspends; power off the controller independent of wake

Some USB hubs let the downstream bus idle (no SOF) while the host is awake; the
dongle sees that as a USB suspend. Since 0.7.0 a suspend immediately powered off the
DualSense's BT, so behind those hubs the controller dropped or never connected
(#174, #148).

Rework the suspend handling so the link survives:

* Debounce the power-off: commit it only after the suspend persists past
  WAKE_POWEROFF_DEBOUNCE_US (3s), so a transient hub suspend -- cancelled by
  tud_resume_cb / tud_mount_cb when the bus returns -- no longer kills the link.

* Treat a deliberate Reconnect USB (FUNC_RECONNECT) as not a host sleep: a grace
  window makes the suspend it induces ignored, so reconnect never drops the
  controller, regardless of the debounce length.

* Run the power-off regardless of enable_wake -- it is a battery-save for a genuine
  host sleep/shutdown; enable_wake now gates only the wake-up keystroke. (The legacy
  non-wake build keeps the simple gate; it has no debounce to filter hub blips.)

* While the host is USB-suspended, keep the dongle on the bus across controller
  power-cycles -- never hide and re-show -- so a controller returning mid-sleep
  cannot re-enumerate and hotplug-wake the host when wake is off.

Default behaviour on a direct connection is unchanged.
